post.title: A drawer for every part
post.body:
The lake on the front of this site is built from parts: pines, boulders, clouds, a moon, a fisherman in a paper boat, and a cast of animals that wander in. The Parts Catalog is where every one of those pieces lives on its own, running live with the same code the scene uses, so I can find it, check it and change it without opening the whole lake.

There are 60 parts in 9 groups. 40 run live, 17 are reference pictures of older versions, and 3 are still in progress. A search box narrows them as you type, and every part has its own link.

## The animals

The animals are the heart of it. 15 origami creatures are rigged at the joints, so a deer can lower its head to graze, look up when something moves, or walk off the card. Between them there are about 17 behaviours and 9 short stories that chain them together. Each card has the controls the scene has: season, day or night, behaviour, and weather. Pick winter and the coats change; pick a blizzard and snow sticks to their backs. Rain beads on them too.

## One loop for forty cards

Forty live cards could easily melt a phone. They all share one animation loop, and any card that isn't on screen sleeps until it scrolls back.

## What I cut

I cut something here too. There used to be a toggle between flat silhouettes and origami. The origami won, so the silhouettes went.

> The origami won, so the silhouettes went.

## The deep-sea header

The header came last: a deep-sea scene with Marley floating in a jellyfish, a diver beside her, and two dozen creatures I lifted out of the painting so they could move on their own, down to an anglerfish with a glowing lure. A whale was the first idea and a dead end. A giant paper squid took its place.

What I learned: build the parts where you can see them alone. A deer that looks right on its own card looks right on the lake, and when something breaks, there's exactly one drawer to open.

episode.title: A drawer for every part
episode.script:
This one is about drawers.

You know the lake on the front of Christian's website. The pines, the boulders, the little fisherman in his paper boat, the animals that wander in. Every one of those pieces also lives somewhere on its own, and that place is the Parts Catalog. Sixty parts in nine groups. Forty of them running live, right there on the page, with the same code the lake uses. It's like opening a box of buttons and finding every one of them moving.

***

The animals are the heart of it. Fifteen origami creatures, each one rigged at the joints. So a deer can lower her head to graze, look up when something stirs, and walk right off the card. About seventeen things they can do, and nine short stories that string them together.

And you can play with them. Change the season, and their coats change. Set it to night. Send a blizzard, and the snow sticks to their backs. Send rain, and it beads up on them, as if they'd been caught out without an umbrella.

***

Here's the clever part. Forty cards all moving at once would cook a phone. So they share a single heartbeat, one loop, and any card you've scrolled past goes quietly to sleep until you come back. It's the kind of care nobody sees, and everybody feels.

And he let things go. There used to be a switch between flat silhouettes and the origami. The origami won, and the silhouettes were retired. Knowing what to let go of is a talent.

***

Then the header. Under the sea, of all places. Marley floating along inside a jellyfish, perfectly at home. A diver beside her. Two dozen creatures lifted right out of the painting so they can swim on their own, down to an anglerfish with a small glowing lantern on its head.

The first idea was a whale. It didn't work. So a giant paper squid took its place, and now I can't imagine it any other way.

***

Looking back, the lesson is in the drawers themselves. Build every part where you can see it on its own. If the deer looks right in her own drawer, she'll look right on the lake. And if something breaks, there's only one drawer to open.
